idiom_name: symantic object of callables (sym.add(sym.lit(1), ...)) passed as a parameter
implementation_notes: Duck typing removes the need for a type class: the algebra is any object exposing the operations, the program is a function taking that object (`def exp(sym): return sym.add(sym.lit(1), sym.add(sym.lit(2), sym.lit(4)))`), and each interpreter is a small class whose methods define one meaning. What replaces the classic structure: an ordinary parameter, optionally documented by `typing.Protocol` (PEP 544) so a type checker sees the contract; higher-kinded emulation (`returns`' `Kind`/`@kinded`) is only worth it when the program itself must be typed as polymorphic in F, which Python never enforces at run time. Justified for testable side-effect boundaries and multi-target rendering in ordinary application code; there is no reason to build a type-level layer.
code_sketch:
class Sym(Protocol):                        # the algebra (structural, optional at run time)
    def lit(self, i: int) -> Any: ...
    def add(self, lhs: Any, rhs: Any) -> Any: ...

def exp(sym: Sym) -> Any:                  # the program: interpretation is a parameter
    return sym.add(sym.lit(1), sym.add(sym.lit(2), sym.lit(4)))

class Eval:                                # interpreter -> int
    lit = staticmethod(lambda i: i)
    add = staticmethod(lambda a, b: a + b)

exp(Eval())   # 7      ; exp(PrettyPrint()) -> '(1 + (2 + 4))'
pitfalls: Nothing enforces the algebra at import time: a Protocol is checked only by static tooling, and even `@runtime_checkable` verifies attribute presence only, never signatures - a wrong arity fails mid-program.
Assigning plain functions as class attributes makes them bound methods (the interpreter's `self` appears as the first argument): use `staticmethod` or module-level objects.
Async interpreters force the whole program to be `async`, so the choice of interpreter leaks into call sites; keep all interpreters of one algebra on the same side.
A module-level singleton interpreter carries state across tests; build the interpreter per test, or pass a recording one explicitly.
